title: Knowledge check — 5 questions
note: Unlocks after the applied activity is submitted. Retakes are free and unlimited.

questions.prompt: Why does the publicly available picture of AI adoption in HR skew toward success and completion?
options: Publications are legally required to report only verified implementations
The people motivated to publish are vendors, consultancies, and practitioners with a win to describe — nobody publishes the ambiguous result, which is the modal one
Failed implementations are rare enough that they don't affect the average
Survey methodology in HR research systematically oversamples large organizations
questions.explanation: A selection effect, not a conspiracy: the content environment is assembled from the subset of experiences someone had a reason to publicize. C is contradicted by the business-value data, and D describes a different problem than the one this lesson is about.

questions.prompt: A large majority of HR leaders report their organizations have not realized significant business value from AI tools. What does this most directly indicate?
options: That AI tools do not work for HR use cases
That the surveyed organizations have not adopted AI at all
That adoption and payoff are separate milestones, and most of the field currently sits in the gap between them
That HR leaders are poor judges of business value
questions.explanation: The finding is about the distance between two milestones, not about the technology's ceiling. B confuses this statistic with the no-plans figure; A over-reads a snapshot of an early field.

questions.prompt: Around nine in ten CHROs expect more AI adoption while over half of organizations have implemented none. What kind of gap is that, and why does it matter?
options: A peer gap — it means your competitors are ahead and you should accelerate
An expectations gap — the pressure is coming from executives rather than peer reality, and it's closed by a conversation with evidence, not by faster buying
A measurement gap — CHROs are counting adoption differently than practitioners
A vendor gap — it shows vendors have oversold to executives specifically
questions.explanation: The distinction is the module's central practical point: the two pressures feel identical and have opposite correct responses. Buying faster does not close a gap between what your executive expects and what is actually possible — it adds a failed implementation to it.

questions.prompt: Of the four errors comparison-driven adoption produces, which one most directly prevents you from ever proving an implementation worked?
options: Adopting what's marketed rather than what fits your function
Mistaking pilots launched for progress
Buying before you can evaluate
Skipping the baseline
questions.explanation: Without a before-number, a working implementation and a useless one are indistinguishable afterward — and the case for your function in Module 7 cannot be built at all. B is a related error but it substitutes a bad metric rather than eliminating the possibility of a good one.

questions.prompt: What does this module actually argue about urgency?
options: That the technology is overhyped and HR functions should wait for it to mature
That you have more room to be deliberate than the content environment suggests, and deliberateness is what separates implementations that survive from ones that get retired
That market pressure on the HRBP role is exaggerated and can be safely discounted
That AI adoption decisions should be deferred to executives who feel the pressure most
questions.explanation: The correction is against comparison-driven haste, not against the technology or against urgency in general. C is explicitly contradicted — Module 2 takes the market pressure on this role seriously and unflinchingly.
